label: Dating and Discernment
framing: Dating is not in the Bible, but discernment is, and so is the kind of love Scripture means to build toward. The question is less whether the feeling is strong than whether the person beside you is honest, kind, and walking the same direction you are.
cultural: Most marriages in the ancient world were arranged by families, with land and lineage at stake and the couple consulted last if at all. Our culture has swung to the opposite pole, treating attraction as the whole of guidance and the self as the only authority, which is why so many capable people feel adrift. Scripture corrects both, refusing to reduce a person to a transaction or to a feeling.
historical: The Christian idea that two people should freely consent to marry, against a family's command if need be, took centuries to win and reshaped the West. Augustine in the fourth century warned how desire deceives the one in its grip, and the Puritans, often caricatured as cold, insisted that mutual love and friendship should precede the vows, not merely follow them.
application: Watch character over chemistry, since chemistry fades and character is what you will live beside for forty years. Notice how the person treats the people they owe nothing, and whether their stated faith can be seen on a Tuesday. Bring others into the discernment rather than trusting your own heart alone, which Scripture says is easily fooled. And guard your body and theirs, not from fear but because love does not rush what it cannot yet promise.

verses.text: The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.”
verses.where: Before there is any sin in the story, God names one thing that is not good: the man's being alone. The site's note says the rest of the chapter answers that sentence, and that the one-flesh union of marriage answers it in every generation. The plain note adds that a single person is not half a person, since Jesus and Paul were single, and that God's compassion for the lonely is the church's calling too.

verses.text: O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.
verses.where: For the third time the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right, and then she says that love is as strong as death. The site's note gives the readings of the refrain: a call to patience and chastity, a request not to disturb the lovers, and wisdom that love should not be forced or stirred up artificially. The woman who speaks it is not ashamed of desire; she knows it is strong enough to be handled with care.

verses.text: But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.”
verses.where: Samuel is impressed by Jesse's tall eldest son, but the LORD tells him that people see the outward appearance while the LORD sees the heart. The youngest son, called in from the sheep, is the one God has chosen. Attraction is real and the Bible gives a whole book to love poetry, but appearance is a poor guide to the person you will live beside for fifty years.

verses.text: Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
verses.where: The book of Proverbs closes with a poem in praise of a wife of noble character, and its center is this verse: charm deceives and beauty fades, but the one who fears the LORD is to be praised. The site's note says the poem is praise, not a performance standard, and that what it prizes most, the fear of the LORD, is open to every believer, man or woman. It is a picture of what to value in anyone you might marry.

verses.text: They called Rebekah and asked her, “Will you go with this man?” “I will go,” she replied.
verses.where: Abraham's servant asked God for a sign at the well, and the site's note points out that the sign he chose tested character: a woman who would draw water for a stranger's ten camels would be generous and hardworking. When her family asks Rebekah whether she will go with him, she answers in a single word, and the note says the decision to leave was hers. Scripture records her consent.

verses.text: And now do not be afraid, my daughter. I will do for you whatever you request, since all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character.
verses.where: At the threshing floor Ruth asks Boaz to marry her, and he blesses her kindness and promises to act, because everyone in his town knows she is a woman of noble character. The site's note says the scene was charged and risky, that Ruth placed her reputation in Boaz's hands, and that he responded with honor rather than advantage. Someone worth marrying protects your good name when they could take advantage of it.

verses.text: Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.
verses.where: Paul describes love by what it does and refuses to do: it is patient and kind, not self-seeking and not easily angered. That makes it a fair test of a relationship over many ordinary days, not of a feeling on one good evening. The site's plain note says plainly that this chapter never asks anyone to hide abuse or stay where they are in danger, and that covering up harm is not love.

verses.text: And this is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that you may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ,
verses.where: From prison Paul tells the Philippians what he prays for them: that their love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that they can test and prove what is best. In his prayer love grows sharper as it grows, not blinder. That is the love to ask God for before deciding whom to marry.

verses.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
verses.where: Paul sets the fruit of the Spirit against the works of the flesh, and the fruit he lists is a character: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. It grows slowly and shows most on hard days. It is a better guide to a future husband or wife than chemistry alone, and a fair mirror for the one doing the looking.

verses.text: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?
verses.where: Paul warns believers not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, and many churches teach from this verse, with Paul's word that a widow may marry one who belongs to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39), that a believer should marry only a believer. The site's plain note says the verse does not ask anyone to leave a spouse or to keep away from people who do not share their faith, and that Christians differ on how far it reaches. The topic on dating a nonbeliever takes the question further.

misread.taken: In much Christian advice about dating, guard your heart is taken to mean holding back feeling, avoiding attachment, or treating any affection before an engagement as a danger, and some have carried it into a lasting fear and shame about love itself.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says that in Hebrew thought the heart was not mainly the seat of emotion. It was the center of the inner person, where a person thinks, decides, remembers and desires, the mind and will together, and guarding it means guarding one's whole inner orientation, the spring from which choices, words and actions flow. The father goes on to guard his son's mouth, eyes and feet as well. It is a call to keep watch over what you love and where you are going, not a command to feel nothing.
misread.text: Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life.

whole: If the person you are dating frightens you, checks your phone, decides whom you may see, pressures you sexually or threatens you, those are warning signs of abuse, and loving them harder will not fix it. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. For most people dating is less dramatic than that, and still heavier than they admit. There is the hope and nerves of a first evening, the long quiet when no one asks, the friends whose engagements arrive one after another, the family asking when, and the fear that one wrong choice will cost the rest of your life. Christians add their own questions: whether dating is even the right way to go about it, whether God has picked out one person, how far is too far, and how to tell love from loneliness.

The Bible has no word for dating. Most marriages in its pages were arranged by families, though Scripture takes care to record Rebekah's own consent. What it has is wisdom about desire, character and discernment, and it is honest about why choosing goes wrong. We see the outward appearance, as Samuel did, and miss the heart. Desire is strong enough to carry us past what we should have noticed; the Song warns not to awaken love before its time for that reason. Loneliness can make a poor match look like rescue, and fear can make a good one look like a trap. And most of us are far quicker to see another person's faults than our own, which is why the people who love us often see more clearly than we do.

So the Bible's wisdom for dating is mostly the wisdom of seeing truly. Date as someone who may one day make a promise, and look for the things a promise will need: the fruit of the Spirit, how the person treats people who can do nothing for them, how the two of you argue and make peace, whether your faith is shared at the root, and whether you are both becoming people who can keep a vow. Give it enough time to see each other on bad days. Ask the counsel of people who know you both, and listen when they hesitate. Keep your bodies in holiness and honor, which protects people rather than shaming them. Honor the other person's freedom, as Rebekah's family asked her and Boaz guarded Ruth's name. And treat the warning signs of control or harm as what they are, not as a problem of fit to be prayed away.

The hope beneath all of this is not that the right person will complete you. God said it was not good for the man to be alone, and that compassion reaches every lonely person, married or single; Jesus, who never married, lived the fullest human life there has been. Where marriage comes, Scripture says it pictures Christ's own love for his church, a love that gives itself up for the other. Where it does not come, or not yet, your life is not on hold, and you are not half a person. Either way you are known and loved by God already, and the love that lays down its life for another is the measure for every relationship you will ever have.
deep.sit: What would the people who love you most say about the way this person treats you, and about who you are when you are with them?

prayer.lead: David asks to be taught God's way and given an undivided heart. Pray it before deciding whom to give your heart to.
prayer.text: Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name. I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart; I will glorify Your name forever.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
Tell someone you trust and get help.
What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.
Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
